newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Zedillo vows to defend sovereignty.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Zedillo vows to defend sovereignty.

text.p: Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo vowed to defend the nation's sovereignty late Thursday in his strongest statement to date surrounding the U.S. drug war certification controversy.
Zedillo responded angrily to a move by a U.S. House of Representatives committee move to try to overturn President Bill Clinton's certification of Mexico as an ally in the war on drugs.
Zedillo suggested the Congressional move could cool the warm ties between both nations, and and pledged to defend Mexico's honor if the U.S. Congress passes the resolution.

"The Mexican government will act with all its might to defend the dignity and the sovereignty of all Mexicans...(I hope) this issue is resolved without forcing us to react vigorously," Zedillo told representatives from 13 Latin American countries in the Caribbean resort of Cancun.
Zedillo said Mexico has shown it is fully cooperating in the drug fight and praised Clinton as "a true friend" of Mexico for recognizing those efforts.

The Congressional committee voted on Thursday to overturn Clinton's finding that Mexico is fully cooperating in the anti-drug war, but to waive the imposition of sanctions against the Mexican government.
Over administration objections, the International Relations Committee voted 27-5 to send the measure to the full House for action. Similar legislation has been introduced in the Senate.

Under a 1961 law, Congressional disapproval of Clinton's certification last Friday that Mexico is an anti-drug ally automatically triggers a ban on U.S. aid and requires votes against multilateral development bank assistance to Mexico.
But the panel and many members of Congress are unwilling to go that far, fearing such action might provoke Mexico to cut off all cooperation in the fight against drug trafficking.
